All of humanity may once have fit inside one high school gym. Not a city. Not a country. One gym.
We picture history as a steady climb. More people, more tools, more progress. But around nine hundred thousand years ago, the climb nearly stopped.
Scientists who read the history hidden in modern DNA estimated that our ancestors crashed to roughly twelve hundred and eighty breeding adults.
And they didn't bounce back fast. If the estimate is right, they stayed that small for more than a hundred thousand years.
The climate was swinging hard. Long droughts. Shrinking forests. Food that moved, or vanished.
In a group that small, one bad season, one sickness, one flood could have erased the entire family tree.
Small groups face a quieter danger, too. When everyone is related, everyone shares the same weak spots.
Nature shows how thin that line can be. In 1980, New Zealand's black robin was down to one breeding pair. Every black robin alive today descends from a single female, Old Blue.
Our ancestors made it through the gap. Hundreds of thousands of years later, their descendants, our species, met another kind of human. The Neanderthals.

Between roughly fifty thousand and forty-three thousand years ago, they had children together. If your family comes from outside Africa, around one to two percent of your DNA still comes from them. If you've ever taken a DNA test, you might have seen it.
Not every scientist accepts the gym-sized estimate. But if it's right, all eight billion of us came from a group you could fit in one room.
In a group that small, nobody made it alone. They stayed together. A bit like you, still here at the very end.
So, would you have made it into the twelve hundred and eighty? Yes, or no?
